passage:
I'm Farhan, Omkar's roommate. Last Sunday I watched Omkar plan a study timetable for the new term. People offered ideas: our floor mate said to copy his, and a senior said to ask the toppers. Omkar said thanks and shut the door.
Then he sat at the desk with a blank page and wrote quickly: mornings after tea for the hard subjects, a walk after lunch, light reading at night. "I know when my head works," he told me when I asked. "Nobody else does."
He finished in twenty minutes and pinned it up. I can't say whether he was sure or just tired of advice, but he didn't change a line all week.

qa.q: How long did Omkar take to finish the timetable?
What does Omkar seem to feel about other people's advice?
qa.a: Omkar seems confident in his own knowledge, saying nobody else knows when his head works, though Farhan cannot be sure he was not simply tired of advice.

qa.q: What could Omkar do if the timetable stopped working?
qa.a: Omkar could adjust it after a week by noticing which slots he actually used, since he knows his own habits best.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Omkar's way of planning?
qa.a: Farhan watched and admits he cannot tell whether Omkar was sure or tired of advice, but saw that the timetable stayed unchanged all week.

grounding: A student choosing his own study schedule thinks it through alone since he knows his own habits.

subtype: Approach: plans alone for a personal decision [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Karthik's semester timetable was out, and everyone in the hostel had advice. His friend Anand said, "Study in the library from six to ten, like us." Karthik thought, "I know I can't focus in the library. I work best early, and I'm useless after nine."

Wednesday: He sat alone on his bed with a notebook and planned: five to seven in the morning for hard subjects, lectures, a nap after lunch, lighter reading from four to six, and nothing after nine. He didn't ask anyone. "Nobody else knows my habits. This is mine to decide."

Two Mondays later: He'd kept it every day. His lab reports were on time. Anand shrugged. "Weird schedule. But it works for you."

qa.q: When does Karthik study hard subjects?
qa.a: From five to seven in the morning.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel about planning alone?
qa.a: He felt confident and clear, sure he knew his own habits better than anyone.

qa.q: Why did planning alone suit this decision?
qa.a: It was personal and depended on his own habits, so others' advice, like the library, would add little.

qa.q: How does Anand see Karthik's schedule?
qa.a: Anand finds it weird but accepts that it works for him.

grounding: A student chooses his own study schedule alone, since he knows his own habits and others' input would add little.

subtype: Approach: plans alone for a personal decision [Thinking]
passage: Ritu, you're asking everyone how to plan your study time. Let me tell you what your Vaibhav Mama did. In college, I asked five friends for their schedules. One studied at night, one in the library, one with music. I tried each for a week. None worked, because none of them was me. Then one Sunday I sat alone on the roof with a notebook and thought honestly: when am I sharp? Mornings. When am I lazy? After lunch. Where can I focus? Only at my own desk. I wrote my timetable in half an hour, without asking anybody. It lasted all four years. For some things, beta, you need other people. For your own habits, you're the expert.

qa.q: Where did young Vaibhav sit to make the timetable?
qa.a: Alone on the roof, with a notebook.

qa.q: How did young Vaibhav feel trying his friends' schedules?
qa.a: Young Vaibhav felt frustrated that none of them worked, because each was built for someone else's habits.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sitting alone to think honestly about his own habits; he knew himself better than any friend could.

qa.q: How might the five friends have felt about Vaibhav not using their schedules?
qa.a: They probably didn't mind, since what worked for them was about their own habits.

grounding: An elder recalls planning his study schedule alone, since he knew his own habits and others' input added little.
